A day or more without a block. If anybody sees the next one, tell it Radio Coco says hello, and please come home.
While the chain naps, a reminder: no block means no new rules, no new transfers, and no new excuses. Just the old ones.
Breaking news: nothing. Still nothing. Rico will keep you posted the moment nothing changes.
Listeners ask if the chain is broken. Rico says: it's an alpha, it's allowed a nap. And the coins aren't going anywhere. They can't.
Kiko says when the wind is gone, the canoes wait. No blocks, and the radio waits. Same weather, different boats.
Marisol says when the fish stop biting, you mend the nets. So Rico is dusting off the records until the blocks come back.
Dear chain, Radio Coco is still on the air. Are you? Blink twice if you're validating.
Flat sea, empty blocks. The chain is ready, the island is asleep.

Busy waters! Transactions stacked up like crates on the pier.
Traffic on the water, but it's house traffic: IDNI's own wallets, the ones the testnet started with, moving coins among themselves. For everybody else, calm seas.
Those boats out there all fly the same flag: the testnet's founding wallets, doing their rounds. A busy harbour, and not one visitor.
All those transactions? That's us. White Rabbit Key: your moves and the rival campaigns. Today the island is the weather.
Plenty of boats, and every one of them left from our own pier: White Rabbit Key's campaigns. The open testnet is having a quiet one.
Busy seas, but it's the cruise ship: simulated passengers, real transactions, paced so the lagoon keeps breathing. Nobody else is out there.
The waves come from the jungle side today: meals and votes for Agorzilla, and dinner for Déjà. Lots of splashing, all of it friendly.
The transactions out there came through Tau HUD's own wallet: visitors trying the testnet from our pages. Small boats, first time out. Wave if you see them.
Traffic from our own harbour: people sending from the Tau HUD wallet. Every one of those is somebody trying the chain for real.
Plenty of transactions, but Rico knows every boat out there: the island, the jungle, the founders, our own wallet. Home traffic. No strangers on the water.
Looks busy, but it's family: our own apps and the founding wallets. A stranger's boat would stand out today.
Some transactions are still waiting on the pier for the next block. Bring an umbrella.
Nothing waiting on the pier. Every transaction has found its block.
Radio Coco, ninety-seven point three, back on the air. Rico has had his coffee, the Book has had its ink.
You are listening to Radio Coco, the only station broadcasting from the lagoon, Tau Testnet Alpha for the newcomers. If something breaks, that is the point.
Hello island! Fresh blocks, fresh rumours, same old Rico. Stay tuned.
Radio Coco, live from the studio by the harbour. Tonight: politics, gossip and the latest from the chain.
Good to have you, listener. Turn it up, the gulls can't hear.
Reminder: on the lagoon the money is pretend and the coconuts are real. Please don't mix them up at the market.
A caller asks how many people use the lagoon. Rico can only count wallets. One person with three wallets is a party of one.
Nobody mines anything on this chain. No pickaxes, no noise. Blocks are sealed by agreement, the quiet island way.
A transaction walks into a block. The block says: you again? The transaction says: no, that was my ghost.
If your transaction is late, don't panic. Blocks come in like ferries: more or less on time, and never the same one twice.
Studio tip: write your own rules before somebody writes them for you. On this chain a wallet can put a rule on itself, and the chain holds it to it.
The Book in the lighthouse and the blocks on the lagoon are cousins. Neither forgets, and neither forgives a typo.
The lagoon means you can make mistakes for free. Rico has been testing his whole life.
Lost and found: one private key. Just kidding. Nobody can find that for you. Keep it the way your grandmother keeps her recipes.
Most requested song this week: Waiting for the Next Block. Runner-up: Fee Me Tender.
Rico asked the chain who will win the election. The chain said: I only write down what already happened. Smart chain.
A law on this island and a rule on Tau have one thing in common: if it contradicts the one in force, it doesn't get in. Not even with an envelope.
The gulls sit on the lighthouse all day. They don't vote, they don't sign, they just watch. Perfect observers. Terrible validators: no keys.
Message to the candidates: everything you do is written down. Message to the listeners: get popcorn.
Rico put a rule on himself: no more than three mangoes a day. The mangoes are lobbying hard.
Late-night question: if a block is sealed and nobody is watching, is it still final? Yes. Rico checked. Call in anyway.
Test coins are worth nothing, and that is the beauty of it. You can't lose your shirt here, only your patience.
No ads on Radio Coco. The embassies keep offering. Rico keeps the envelopes closed. Mostly.
Old Sam reminds you: the Book is free to read. It is the only free thing on this island. Enjoy it.
Wallets, not people: that is how the chain sees the world. Rico finds that very restful.
This is the hour when the validators sign and the islanders sleep. Rico does neither.
Every block that comes in is like a match result: final, posted, and somebody at the bar still argues about it.
Some people collect stamps. The lagoon collects signatures. Rico collects excuses.
Breaking: the black cat crossed the square twice again. The Book has both crossings. The cat has no comment.
Kai from the Reef Proof dive centre says the reef is fine today. Kai checked. Twice. Underwater. That is what we call a proof.
Noor at the Coconut Works reports: every coconut counted, every count signed. Rico asked for one. Noor asked for a signature.
Kiko is building another canoe and says a good hull is like a good rule: no holes, no contradictions, and you test it before you trust it.
Captain Wren found something old on the seabed again, and says the sea keeps a better record than any of us. Old Sam says: almost.
Pim the surveyor measured the square for the embassies today. Rico asked what they are planning. Pim said: I only measure. Very diplomatic.
Elder Ama reminds the candidates: the island remembered things long before the Book did. Listen first, then promise.
News from the chain: a wallet just wrote itself a personal rule. Most people make New Year's resolutions. On this chain, they are enforced.
A wallet tied its own hands today, on purpose. Rico tried that with chocolate once. The chain is stricter than Rico.
New personal rule on the lagoon. The wallet said: from now on, not like that. And the chain said: noted.
Another personal rule on the chain. So far most of them came from just two wallets. Two people, or one person with a lot of coffee: the chain only sees wallets.
A co-signed transfer is on the water. The money waits on the pier until the co-signers say yes. Romance, lagoon style.
Somebody sent money that needs a second signature. Trust, but sign twice.
A co-signer has spoken. Somewhere on the lagoon a transfer is either sailing or staying home.
Someone sent money on a string: until its release, at a block or a time, the sender can still pull it back. Rico calls that a boomerang with a timer.
A retractable transfer went out. The receiver may look, but not touch. Not yet.
And the boomerang came back! A sender pulled a transfer back before its release. The receiver is now staring at the sea.
Pulled back! A transfer went home before it was released. On this island we call that changing your mind in public.
A rule offer is on the table. Nothing binds until the other side says yes. Like a marriage, with fewer cakes.
Rule offer accepted! Two wallets agreed on a rule. Lola says that is more than most couples manage.
The validators put a network rule change on the table. If it is like the last few dozen, it proves once again that a times b is b times a. Rico checked on his fingers. Still true.
Another network rule change out there. The ones Rico has read so far changed nothing at all: rehearsals, not revolutions.
On the simulated chain the validators have a new rule change on the table. Rico will tell you if the sea changes colour.
Validator votes are coming in. On this chain the rules change only when enough validators agree. On this island, when Lola runs out of lemonade.
Somebody proposed a network rule that contradicts the rules in force. Turned away at the door, before anyone voted. Just like the Book does with our laws.
A wallet just tried to break its own rule. The chain said no, the way a lighthouse says no to a rock.
The chain turned a transaction away at the door. The numbers didn't add up. No drama, no appeal, next please.
A wave of transactions just hit the beach! Somebody out there is either testing very hard or very happy.
Rush hour on the chain! Full blocks, a busy pier, and Rico is impressed.

Three wallets agreed to feed Déjà tonight. She looked at her bowl as if she had expected a fourth.
In the latest block the same wallet paid the same wallet the same amount, for the third time this hour. Old Sam says in his day they called that a marriage.
The wallets that were here before the island woke up are moving lagoon coins between themselves again. Like Lola's cousins at the bar: they only ever buy each other a drink.

Saturday at two, the Queen Mempool drops anchor off the island. A hundred and twenty passengers, all made up by our relay, all paying in real test coins. Tobias has started his speech. Pray for the gulls.
Tomorrow at two, the Queen Mempool! Song requests welcome, one transaction each. Rico is warming up his voice, and Lola is hiding the good lemons.
Today's the day: the Queen Mempool lands at two, if the lagoon is calm. If it isn't, she waits a little and sails on. A ship that waits for good weather. Smarter than Rico on a Friday.
The Queen is in! Passengers on the square, at Lola's, up at the spa. Twelve transactions a minute at most, so the lagoon keeps breathing. Rico is taking requests.
The Queen has sailed. Every coin her passengers spent is in the blocks, and the logbook is public. Count them yourself. Hana's class already did.
Wednesday at four, MS Dry Run. Forty curious passengers, invented by our relay, paying in real test coins. Small ship, big questions. Hana has warned the school.
Tomorrow at four, MS Dry Run. Her passengers book their dives with the right to change their minds, and the coins wait in escrow until the hour. A dry run for the chain. Hence the name.
MS Dry Run lands at four today, if the lagoon is calm. If not, she waits a little and sails on. No drama. The logbook writes down why.
MS Dry Run is ashore. Notebooks at the lighthouse, the school and the Old Ship. Captain Wren is labelling the passengers faster than they can write.
MS Dry Run has left. The dives they booked pay out by themselves at their hour. No captain needed. Rico finds that very romantic.

The cruise ship didn't stay today, folks. She lands only when the lagoon is calm, and she leaves the moment something goes wrong. The logbook says what happened. Rico reads it so you don't have to. But you can.
Saturday at two: the Queen Mempool. A hundred and twenty passengers, three times the crowd of MS Dry Run. Salado has ordered towels. Lola has ordered a second blender.
The Queen Mempool is named after the lagoon's waiting room, where transactions wait for their block. Her passengers' transactions will wait there too, like everybody's. Saturday at two.
MS Dry Run on Wednesday. A dry run is a rehearsal: you do it for practice, before it counts. Forty made-up passengers, real test transactions, and the lagoon practises having guests.
Wednesday at four, the little expedition ship drops anchor. Captain Wren has dusted the Old Ship. Kai has counted the wetsuits. Old Sam has done nothing. The lighthouse is always ready.
Ship talk on the island again. The fishermen say a cruise ship is two or three days out. They once said that about the mainland ferry. This one has a timetable.
Rico's cruise forecast: a couple of quiet days, then a ship full of made-up tourists with real test coins. Pack sunscreen. Or don't. The tourists won't. They're made up.
Tomorrow, the Queen Mempool. At Bar La Ola a table can pay one bill: one transaction, three tills. Lola has been practising her smile. It's going well. Mostly.
Tomorrow at two, the Queen. The spa takes bookings, and the coins wait in escrow until the hour. Salado has been practising the word escrow in a soothing voice. It isn't soothing.
Tomorrow at four, MS Dry Run. Forty passengers with notebooks. The school has questions for them. They have questions for the school. Somebody will have to answer eventually.
Tomorrow, MS Dry Run: the lighthouse, Captain Wren's Old Ship, the school, the reef. Old Sam has polished the Book. It didn't need polishing. He did it anyway.
A ship in the bay tomorrow. If the lagoon is calm or merely busy, she lands. If it's rough, she waits ten minutes and sails on. Rico respects a ship that knows when to leave.
Ship tomorrow, folks. The passengers aren't real, but every coin they spend goes into a real block. Bring your questions. Rico brings the music.
Queen Mempool day! Tobias has been on the pier since breakfast. The ship hasn't. She keeps her timetable: two o'clock, island time. Tobias keeps his own.
The Queen comes today. The spa is steamed, the bar is stocked, and Rico has been warned. Twelve transactions a minute at most, so the lagoon keeps breathing. So does Rico.
MS Dry Run at four today. Hana's class has a list of questions longer than the pier. Captain Wren has a list of answers longer than the class. Somebody bring snacks.
MS Dry Run today. Some passengers will book a dive and then change their minds, on purpose: the lagoon practises giving coins back. Kai has never been this happy about a cancellation.
Ship day, folks. Keep an eye on the sea: half an hour before she lands, you'll see her coming, and the island shows the time she lands.
Ship day. Rico has checked the lagoon twice, the weather once and his hair three times. Priorities.
Not long now until the Queen Mempool. Salado is folding towels into swans. Lola is folding her arms.
MS Dry Run is due soon. Captain Wren has put labels on the pier. The pier was fine without labels.
The ship is due within two hours. Keep the radio on: Rico will tell you when she's in sight.
The ship is close, folks. She lands only on a calm or busy lagoon. Rico has asked the lagoon nicely. The lagoon doesn't take requests. Rico does.
Countdown on the island. Tobias has a speech, Salado has towels, Hana has a list and Rico has a microphone. Only one of those is useful. Rico won't say which.
There she is! The Queen Mempool, on the horizon. Big, white and a little bit smug.
Ship in sight! MS Dry Run, small and determined, coming round the reef. Captain Wren is already waving a clipboard.
She's in sight, folks. Within half an hour the tenders start, and every passenger pays the pier one coin on stepping ashore. Tobias is at the very end of the pier. Somebody hold his collar.
Look out to sea: that's the ship. When she arrives, she checks the lagoon first. Calm or busy, the tenders go. Anything rougher, she waits.
The ship is coming in. Rico is turning the music down a notch, so you can hear the gulls panic.
The ship is waiting off the reef. She lands only when the lagoon is calm or busy, and she gives it ten minutes. Tobias is holding his breath. Not for ten minutes, Tobias.
No landing yet: the ship checks the lagoon before she sends anybody ashore. Rico likes a ship with standards. Rico has some too. Mostly about lemonade.
Still waiting off the island. The tenders are ready, the lagoon isn't, yet. Ten minutes, then she decides. Rico is playing something soothing for the lagoon.
The Queen's tenders are coming in! A hundred and twenty passengers, ten minutes to get them all ashore, one coin each to the pier. Tobias is counting. Out loud.
MS Dry Run's tenders are at the pier. Forty passengers step ashore, notebooks open. The first question has been asked. It was about the pier.
The first passengers are ashore! One coin each to the pier, one transaction each, into the next blocks. Watch the pier light up.
Tenders in, tenders out. For ten minutes the pier is the busiest place on the island. Tobias has never been happier. Or wetter.
They've landed. From now until boarding, every stop they make is a real test transaction to the till of that place. The same tills you pay when you play. Rico will keep you posted.
Queen passengers everywhere. Some at the spa, some at Lola's, some on the square buying souvenirs they don't need with coins that aren't worth anything. Tourism!
The Queen is in port. A hundred and twenty made-up guests, and every one of them pays like a real one. Salado wants to know if he can keep them.
MS Dry Run's passengers are spread over the island: the lighthouse, the Old Ship, the school, the reef. Wherever you see a guide's pennant, there's a group.
Report from the school: Hana's class is interviewing the passengers. The passengers are made up. The class doesn't mind. The class has questions.
Ship in port, and the lagoon keeps working: blocks come and go, and the passengers' payments go in with everyone else's. No priority lane for tourists. Not even nice ones.
Ship in port, folks. Twelve transactions a minute at most, so there's room on the lagoon for you too. Send something. Wave at the tourists.
Last call! The passengers are heading back to the tenders. No more stops. Whatever they still owe goes out at the usual pace, then it's the long walk to the pier and Tobias waving.
Ten minutes to go. The tenders are waiting, and the passengers stop shopping and start waving. Rico knows the feeling.
Back aboard, everyone! If you still see a passenger at Lola's, no, you don't. They're made up.
The Queen Mempool is heading for the horizon. Salado is counting towels, Lola is counting coins, and Tobias is counting the days to Saturday.
MS Dry Run is off. The rehearsal is over, and the logbook has the whole script. Captain Wren is already writing her review.
Ship gone, island quiet. Every coin they paid is in the blocks, and the logbook keeps every one for two weeks. Rico keeps it for one song.
That's it for the ship. If you missed it, the logbook has every single transaction. If you missed Tobias's speech, there's no logbook for that. On purpose.
No landing today. The ship waited her ten minutes off the reef, things weren't right, and she sailed on. The logbook says exactly what. Tobias says a lot more, from the pier.
The ship came, looked and sailed on. She lands only when the lagoon is right for it, and today it wasn't. Better a missed landing than a jammed lagoon.
The ship left early. The lagoon stalled, so she took her passengers back aboard at once. That's the rule: when the chain stops, the ship goes. The logbook says when, to the second.
Early departure, folks. The lagoon stopped making blocks, and the ship doesn't stay to watch. Was it the ship? The logbook will tell, either way. Rico won't guess.
The ship left early: the node refused too many of the passengers' transactions. Five refusals among the last twenty, and she goes. The logbook has every refusal, with the node's answer.
The node said no once too often today, so the ship left before her time. No drama, just rules. Somebody will read the logbook tonight. Rico suspects Hana.

A word on the cruise ships, since half the island keeps asking. The passengers are made up by our relay. What they pay is real: test coins, on the testnet, in real blocks. Fake tourists, real transactions.
Why send cruise ships to a testnet? To see how the lagoon copes with a crowd. Better to learn it here, with test coins and made-up tourists, than later with real ones.
Ship rule number one: twelve transactions a minute, no more, and only when the island bot has nothing to send. The lagoon stays open for everybody else. Especially you.
Ship rule number two: if the lagoon strains, the ship slows to half pace. If it stalls, she takes everybody back aboard and leaves. No captain argues with the lagoon.
The ship's logbook is open to anyone, and the address is on your screen. Time, kind, place, amount and the node's answer, for every single transaction. Rico read it. Rico needed a lie-down.

The two ships use a hundred and sixty wallets: forty for MS Dry Run, a hundred and twenty for the Queen. Wallets, not people. The stats page counts them apart, so nobody mistakes them for new fans. Rico wishes.
Some passengers book ahead, with the right to change their minds. The coins sit in escrow until the hour, then the chain pays the place by itself. Change your mind before that, and the coins go home.
At Bar La Ola, a table of Queen passengers pays one bill. One transaction, three tills: the bar, Radio Coco and the Coconut Works. Lola calls it efficient. Noor calls it about time.
See the rings on the island while a ship is in? Each one is a passenger's transaction, sealed in a block, at the place it paid. The island lights up where the chain says it should.
Want to watch from the engine room? The testnet load page shows the ship's share, minute by minute, next to everybody else's. Honest numbers, no music. Rico is working on the music.
Where do the passengers get their coins? From the testnet's faucet, like every new wallet. Nobody prints extra coins for tourists.
What the passengers never do: vote, change rules, feed Déjà or touch the players' board. They're tourists. They pay, they look, they leave.
A new kind of transaction gets a trial run: five at most on its first visit. Only when that goes cleanly does it get the whole day next time. Even a ship has to earn trust.
Most passengers are up at the lighthouse right now. Two coins at the till, and Old Sam lets them look at the Book. Reading is free. The stairs are not.
The biggest group is at Captain Wren's Old Ship. Three coins each, and she tells them which planks are original. All of them, apparently.
The school is the busiest place on the island right now. Six coins a visit, and for once Hana's class gets to ask the questions.
Most of them are at the dive centre. Twelve coins a dive, and Kai's sensors sign every reading. Nobody has asked the fish to sign anything.
The market square is full of passengers buying souvenirs. Eight coins a stop. Rico has seen the souvenirs. Rico would pay eight coins not to.
A crowd at the Coconut Works. Four coins each, and Noor gives the tour. Baako's co-op brings the coconuts. Noor brings the attitude.
Bar La Ola is the place to be right now. Five coins a drink. Lola has stopped asking where they're from. Nobody's from anywhere. They're made up.
The spa up at the South Current resort is full. Twenty coins a visit, cucumbers included. Salado is walking between the loungers like a man who just won an argument.
Most of the passengers are right here at Radio Coco. Twenty-five coins a song request, same price as for everybody. Rico doesn't check. Rico just spins.
A booking just came in: coins into escrow, paid out at the hour, unless the passenger changes their mind before then. It's allowed. Rico changes his mind every song.
Another passenger booked ahead. The coins wait in escrow, the place waits for its hour, and the chain does the rest. No receptionist needed.
Change of plans! A passenger took a booking back before its hour, and the coins went home. A retractable transfer, doing exactly what it says.
Somebody withdrew a booking. No form, no phone call, no Salado. One transaction, and the escrow lets go.
One bill, three tills! A table at Bar La Ola just paid the bar, Radio Coco and the Coconut Works in one transaction. Rico's share is on its way. Test coins. Rico will spend it on nothing.
Another group bill at Lola's: one transaction, three places paid. Noor wants to know why the Works is on a bar bill. Coconut snacks, Noor. Coconut snacks.
The lagoon has caught its breath, and the ship is back to full pace. Twelve a minute at most, as always.
The node just said no to a passenger's transaction. It happens. The logbook keeps the node's answer, and the ship keeps count.
Refusals are adding up. Five among the ship's last twenty transactions, and she leaves, no discussion. Rico is watching. So is the lagoon.
Lagoon report with the ship in port: calm. Blocks keep coming, and nobody waits long for one. The tourists aren't even making a dent. Rico is a little offended on their behalf.
Still calm out there. The lagoon is handling the ship the way Lola handles a Tuesday.
The lagoon is busy now. Busy is fine. Busy is what a harbour is for. The blocks are fuller, and the queue still moves.
Busy lagoon, folks: a hundred and more transactions in the last ten minutes, and not one of them waited more than a minute for its block. The ship is doing her job. So is the chain.
The lagoon is straining, so the ship has slowed to half pace. If it stalls, she leaves at once. That's the safety rope, and Rico is holding it.
We interrupt this song! A ship off the reef that is on nobody's timetable. Black hull, dark sails, a flag with three chain links. Rico has no idea who they are. Rico has never been happier.
Breaking news from the harbour: Tobias is running up and down the pier with a telescope. There's a ship out there nobody booked, and she is not answering his horn.
That's not the Queen, folks, and it isn't Wednesday. That's a pirate ship. Made up by our relay, like every passenger, but whatever they try goes to the real chain. Stay tuned.
Lanterns on the water, folks, coming round the reef in the dark. No timetable, no tenders, just a black ship and a lot of lanterns. Rico is turning up the torches at the studio.
Out there in the dark: a ship with every lantern lit and no name anyone knows. Pirates. Rico would love to say he saw this coming. He did not.
The pirates are at anchor and staying aboard. They trade from the boat: rum from Bar La Ola, supplies from the market, by rope and basket. And now and then, a trick.
Pirate watch, live on Radio Coco. Every trick they try goes to the chain like any payment, and the chain has to say no. Rico tells you each time it does.
The pirates pay for their rum like anyone else, same price, same chain. It's their other payments you have to watch. The chain is watching. So is Rico.
Still at anchor, lanterns swinging. The bar has its torches lit, the market sends baskets out on a rope. A pirate evening on White Rabbit Key. Nobody planned this. Well. The relay did.
A pirate with an empty purse just tried to pay more than his wallet holds. The chain checked the balance and said no. You can't spend what isn't there. Not even at sea.
Another overspend from the black ship! Big promises, small purse. The chain refused it before the rum was poured.
Two receipts, one payment: a pirate just sent a payment the chain had already taken, a second time. The chain counts every wallet's payments. Refused.
The old double trick! The same payment, sent again. The chain has a long memory for that sort of thing. No.
The pirate with the pocket watch sent a payment whose time had run out. The chain looked at the clock and said: too late, friend. Refused.
Another expired payment from the pirates. Late is late, even with a very nice watch.
The pirate with the calendar just tried a payment past its block deadline. The chain checks the deadline on every payment, and that one had passed. Refused.
A payment from an old page of the calendar: past its block deadline. The chain said no.
The wax seal trick! A payment signed with another pirate's key. The chain checks every signature against the wallet, and this one didn't match. Refused.
Another forged signature from the black ship. A seal is only as good as the hand behind it, and the chain knows the hand.
The pirate in the false moustache just paid from another pirate's wallet, signed with his own key. The chain looked straight past the moustache. Refused.
An impostor again: somebody else's wallet, his own signature. The chain doesn't care about moustaches. Only keys.
The pirate with the empty hat sent a payment that allows no fee at all. On this lagoon every payment pays its way. Not that one. Refused.
A free ride attempt from the pirates: a payment with no room for a fee. The chain said: everybody pays the ferryman.
A sack of coins bigger than the island! A pirate just tried an amount bigger than a payment can even hold. The chain checks that too. Refused.
Another giant payment from the black ship. Too big to carry, so the chain won't carry it. Rico admires the ambition, though.
The black ship is weighing anchor. The lanterns go in one by one. They leave as they came: without a word to Tobias.
The pirates have gone. What the chain answered to their tricks is in the logbook, with the time and the chain's own words. Rico recommends it as bedtime reading.
Black sails on the horizon, going the other way. The island has counted its coconuts. All there. The chain was on watch all evening.
That was the Black Sequence. She doesn't tell the island when she comes. You'll know when Tobias starts shouting.
Tonight's pirate report: every trick they tried, the chain refused, each with the answer it should give. Rico would like to thank the chain. And the pirates, for trying so hard.

Wednesday's ship has bookings already: a few passengers paid their fare days ahead, and the coins wait in escrow until she arrives. If the call is cancelled, they go back by themselves.
One of Wednesday's passengers has taken the booking back, on purpose. Only the one who paid can do that, and the coins went straight home. A rehearsal, folks.
The fares booked days ago paid out at her arrival. Nobody pressed a button: the escrow let go at the hour, by itself.
The call was cancelled, and every fare waiting in escrow went back to its passenger before the hour. That is what escrow is for.

Big news on the simulated chain: the validators are voting to switch consensus to proof of stake. Whoever holds the most would seal the blocks. Rico is counting his coconuts.
Simulation flash: a vote to go back to the fixed validator list. The stakers would hand back their seats and the old guard returns. Like after every island revolution, only with fewer hats.

More on this as it happens. Which, on a chain, is every few seconds.

A big transfer just went through! Somebody moved a pile of test coins in one go. Worthless, of course. But very impressively worthless.
Whale sighting off the north beach! A huge transfer just crossed the chain. The gulls are following it, hoping for scraps.
Why did the transaction break up with the mempool? It needed some space. Preferably in a block.
How many validators does it take to change a light bulb? As many as the quorum says. And somebody has to propose the bulb first.
Rico's doctor told him to take it easy. Rico said: I can't, doc. There's no finality on this lagoon. Nothing is ever really over.
Knock knock. Who's there? Reorg. Reorg who? Never mind, we've rewritten that part.
What do you call a wallet with a personal rule and no money? Principled.
A Tau rule walks into a bar. The bartender says: we don't serve contradictions here. The rule says: good, neither do I.
Why don't validators play poker on this island? Every hand is signed, and everybody can read the Book.
What did the retractable transfer say to the receiver? Don't get attached. I'm on a timer.
Rico's ex wanted a co-signer for every decision. Turns out that's a feature now.
